Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, CD006230. <https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD006230.pub2>; Opposite: Venneman NG, Buskens E, Besselink MG, et al. (2005). Small gallstones are associated with increased risk of acute pancreatitis: potential benefits of prophylactic cholecystectomy? American Journal of Gastroenterology, 100(11), 2540-2550. <https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1572-0241.2005.00317.x>
tips.caveats: This topic is still debated. The exact criteria for those exceptions haven’t been verified yet. Another counterpoint concerns small stones: those under 5 mm are more closely linked to pancreatitis, and Dutch research suggests prophylactic removal might either extend or shorten life depending on how common and severe pancreatitis is in a given population. European guidelines do list two exceptions: porcelain gallbladder and gallstones over 1 cm alongside large polyps — both warrant removal. Removal may also be considered during other major abdominal surgeries. Crucially, this advice applies only to stones inside the gallbladder with no prior symptoms; stones in the common bile duct are a completely different matter. UK and European guidelines both stress that stones in the bile duct must be removed along with the gallbladder, regardless of symptoms. Seek emergency care immediately if you experience persistent upper abdominal pain, fever, chills, yellowing of the eyes or skin, or dark urine. When a doctor recommends surgery after reviewing imaging, ask which specific criteria prompted that decision — whether it’s bile duct involvement, polyps, or abnormal gallbladder walls — so you can weigh those factors against this general guideline, which is meant to discourage surgery without any valid medical reason. Both cited studies tracked patients over 4 to 9 years, focusing on what happens when no intervention is taken; they don’t compare treatment effectiveness. Longer follow-ups would likely show a higher rate of symptom development.

tips.title: Don’t cut calcium out to prevent kidney stones
tips.cost: No cost at all. In fact, it’s easier — no need to constantly watch what foods contain calcium.
tips.inPlainWords: People who’ve had calcium oxalate stones are often advised to limit calcium intake, but randomized trials show the opposite. A study with 120 men who repeatedly developed stones divided them into two groups: one ate a normal amount of calcium while cutting back on animal protein and salt; the other followed a traditional low‑calcium diet. After five years, recurrence rates were 12 out of 60 versus 23 out of 60 — meaning the normal‑calcium group had half the risk. UK guidelines also advise against restricting calcium.
tips.benefit: This five‑year randomized trial enrolled 120 men with recurrent calcium oxalate stones and high urinary calcium levels. One group consumed 30 mmol of calcium daily, reduced animal protein to 52 g per day, and limited salt to 50 mmol of sodium chloride; the control group ate only 10 mmol of calcium daily. Over five years, recurrence occurred in 12/60 versus 23/60 participants. The unadjusted relative risk was 0.49 (95% CI 0.24–0.98; P = 0.04), indicating half the risk with normal calcium intake. Both groups saw a similar drop in urinary calcium — about 170 mg per day — but oxalate excretion fell by 7.2 mg/day in the normal‑calcium group versus a rise of 5.4 mg/day in the low‑calcium group. NICE guideline NG118 states adults should aim for 700–1200 mg of calcium daily; children and teens need 350–1000 mg per day. The perception that cutting calcium is beneficial stems from the intuitive idea that “stones are made of calcium, so less calcium must help.”
tips.sources: Borghi L, Schianchi T, Meschi T, et al. (2002). Comparison of two diets for the prevention of recurrent stones in idiopathic hypercalciuria. New England Journal of Medicine, 346(2), 77-84. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa010369>; National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (2019). Renal and ureteric stones: assessment and management. NICE guideline NG118, clause 1.8.1. <https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng118/chapter/Recommendations>
tips.caveats: Caveats: This trial involved only men with recurrent calcium oxalate stones and high urinary calcium; results may not apply to all stone types. Moreover, the intervention group simultaneously reduced protein and salt intake, so some benefits could stem from those changes rather than calcium alone. This advice specifically discourages actively eliminating calcium‑rich foods — it does not advocate extra calcium supplementation. For any need to add calcium pills, consult your physician. Regarding hydration, see Section 16, Item 8: drinking 2.5–3 L of water daily after a stone episode.

tips.title: Don’t buy crystals, bracelets or “lucky” figurines for good luck, wealth or health benefits
tips.cost: There is no monetary cost involved. The only requirement is to avoid listing “good luck,” “health benefits,” or similar claims as reasons for purchase. The real challenge is resisting the urge to buy them when everyone else is wearing them and talking about their magical powers.
tips.inPlainWords: There is no verifiable evidence that wearing such an item changes your fate, attracts wealth or improves health. The claims work the way fortune-telling does: they are vague enough that anyone can read themselves into them. Where a seller states outright that a stone cures a disease or guarantees money, that is a misleading advertisement under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, and can be complained about to the Central Consumer Protection Authority or a district consumer commission; vague talk of “good luck” is not something any authority can prove false. Buying such an item as decoration is fine; paying extra for the luck is what this entry is about.
tips.benefit: Classic classroom experiments demonstrate that when participants receive the same generic “personality analysis,” they almost universally deem it accurate. This phenomenon is known as the Barnum effect, and it explains why many people feel that wearing these items somehow improves their lives. Forer’s 1949 demonstration is the original version: he handed each of the 39 students in the class the same generic personality sketch while presenting it as an assessment written for that individual. Most of the 39 rated it 4 or 5 on a 0-to-5 scale for how well it described them, and the average rating was about 4.26. The underlying conclusion is simple: personal acceptance of a vague statement does not validate its factual accuracy, and the fact that a description feels accurate says nothing about whether a bracelet, a crystal or any other object changes your health or your luck.
tips.sources: Forer BR (1949). The fallacy of personal validation: A classroom demonstration of gullibility. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology. <https://doi.org/10.1037/h0059240>
tips.caveats: This entry serves one main purpose: to emphasize that there is no scientific basis for any claimed benefits, nor any measurable predictive power. It does not pass judgment on personal beliefs or cultural traditions, nor does it discourage buying such items as gifts, mementos, or family heirlooms. Two points must be clearly distinguished: legally enforceable claims about product performance can be reported to authorities, while vague notions like “good luck” lack any research support and cannot be proven false; thus, personal budget control is the only practical safeguard. Before purchasing, treat the item strictly as a decorative piece and ask yourself: “If it offered no magical benefits at all, would I still pay this price?” For guidance on verifying materials and certifications, or why treating them as investments is unwise, refer to Sections 5.33 and 5.34. Information on spending money on fortune-tellers is provided in Section 5.15.

tips.title: Don’t expect shopping to lift your mood or boost your sense of self-worth
tips.cost: No cost at all. The hard part is resisting the urge to buy things when you’re feeling down.
tips.inPlainWords: On average, people who place a higher value on money and material possessions report lower levels of happiness. This conclusion comes from pooled analyses of hundreds of studies, though the link between the two is fairly weak and it’s unclear which factor drives the other. Other research comparing spending on experiences versus physical goods found that money spent on experiences tends to bring more satisfaction. So when you’re in a bad mood, reallocating your budget toward a day out or a meal with friends is far more likely to help than adding more items to your shopping cart.
tips.benefit: This meta-analysis combined data from 259 independent studies, covering a total of 753 effect sizes. The results showed that individuals who prioritize material possessions tend to report lower happiness levels. On the most commonly used multi-dimensional well‑being scale, the correlation coefficient was r = –0.19 (adjusted ρ = –0.24). When only the single dimension of “valuing money” was measured, the correlation weakened to r = –0.08 to –0.11. The strength of this link varied depending on the specific outcome measured: it was strongest with risky health‑related and consumption behaviors and negative self‑evaluations (r = –0.28 to –0.44) and weakest with overall life satisfaction and negative emotions (r = –0.13 to –0.15). Mediation analyses suggested that this negative relationship may arise because psychological needs remain unmet. Another set of studies asked different groups of participants whether spending on experiences or on goods made them happier; respondents consistently chose experiences. Laboratory experiments confirmed this: recalling a purchase made for an experience produced a better mood than recalling a purchase of a physical item.
tips.sources: Dittmar H, Bond R, Hurst M, Kasser T (2014). The relationship between materialism and personal well-being: A meta-analysis. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 107(5), 879-924. <https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037409>; Van Boven L, Gilovich T (2003). To do or to have? That is the question. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 85(6), 1193-1202. <https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.85.6.1193>
tips.caveats: Caveats: Most of the included studies surveyed the same group of people at a single point in time, so they can’t determine which factor comes first. The authors themselves note that further experiments and long‑term follow‑ups are needed to clarify the direction of this relationship. Therefore, this recommendation should not be interpreted as “shopping makes people unhappy”; rather, it means “relying on shopping to improve your mood is unlikely to succeed.” The overall correlation is modest: r = –0.19 accounts for only a few percentage points of variation, and individual differences are considerable. This advice does not discourage spending on items you genuinely enjoy; it simply warns against using shopping as a mood‑regulation tool, as that can lead to repeated impulse buys when you’re feeling down. Specific ways to save money are described in Section 5. Evidence‑based strategies for coping with low mood can be found in the latter part of Section 22 and in Section 29. Information on budgeting to “outperform” others is covered in Item 24 of this section.

tips.title: Don’t spend extra money to “move up a rung” among your peers by buying a new house, car, or social circle
tips.cost: No cost at all. All you need to do is ask one extra question before increasing your budget: is this extra expense buying a real product, or simply securing a higher status among your peers? The difficulty lies in resisting the urge to upgrade when everyone else does.
tips.inPlainWords: When comparing people with similar incomes, those whose neighbors earn more report lower happiness levels. This effect appears only among neighbors with comparable education and frequent social interaction. Thus, spending extra money to move into a neighborhood where everyone is wealthier actually pushes you down the social ladder. Yet when incomes rise across the board, people still feel better off, so absolute levels of happiness remain relevant.
tips.benefit: The National Survey of Family and Households (NSFH) in the U.S. surveyed the same individuals twice. Researchers matched these results with local average incomes calculated from a 5% sample of the 1990 census. After adjusting for personal characteristics and income, they found that higher neighbor incomes correlate strongly with lower self-reported happiness. This effect holds across multiple analytical methods and remains highly statistically significant. In fact, the drop in happiness caused by a rise in neighbor incomes matches the drop produced by a comparable fall in one’s own income. Even after controlling for individual-level factors or limiting comparisons to the same state and survey round, the pattern persists. This rules out explanations such as happier people naturally moving to poorer areas, unmeasured state-level variables, or differences between renters and homeowners. The effect is strongest among individuals with close neighbor ties, while those who socialize mainly outside their community show no such trend. Happiness declines only when comparing with neighbors of similar education; income differences among less educated neighbors have little impact. The mechanism appears to work mainly through satisfaction with one’s material circumstances rather than other life domains. Finally, when both personal and neighbor incomes rise proportionally, overall happiness still increases.
tips.sources: Luttmer EFP (2005). Neighbors as Negatives: Relative Earnings and Well-Being. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 120(3), 963–1002. <https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/120.3.963>; Luttmer EFP (2004). Relative Earnings and Well-Being. NBER Working Paper No. 10667 (The expressions and magnitudes cited in this article are verified verbatim according to this edition). <https://www.nber.org/papers/w10667>; Indian Council of Medical Research. <https://www.icmr.gov.in/>; World Health Organization. <https://www.who.int/>
tips.caveats: Several reasons justify a B rating: the data come from repeated surveys of the same participants, this is the sole study of its kind, and the sample is foreign; the measured outcome is self-reported happiness rather than monetary figures. Researchers applied multiple statistical controls, such as within-person comparisons and comparisons limited to the same state and survey round, but the study is still not a randomized trial. The benefit magnitude is classified as “moderate” following the criteria established in section 23 (don’t expect material purchases to boost happiness). The potential savings can indeed reach tens of thousands of rupees; however, because no quantitative link exists between those savings and actual happiness gains, they are not classified as “large.” This advice does not discourage spending on larger homes, quieter neighborhoods, or shorter commutes when those features themselves are valued. What it discourages is spending solely to avoid feeling inferior to colleagues or peers. For guidance on how to prioritize housing choices, see section 4, item 18 (give priority to commute time when selecting a residence). For information on using purchases to improve mood, refer to section 23 (don’t expect material purchases to boost happiness). Regarding the tendency to constantly compare oneself with others online, see section 3, item 20 (don’t make “how others are doing” a daily obsession).

tips.title: Don’t believe that “willpower is like a muscle that runs out after use”
tips.cost: No cost at all. All that needs changing is the way we talk about it.
tips.inPlainWords: The popular idea is that after doing something that requires self‑control, it becomes easier to give in to temptation later on, so we should “save” our willpower. Yet extensive multi-laboratory replications using standardized protocols found essentially null results. Stop using “I’ve run out of willpower today” as an excuse, and don’t spend money on courses that promise to help you conserve it.
tips.benefit: In a multi‑lab preregistered replication study, 23 labs with 2,141 participants followed Sripada et al.’s standardised procedure: first they performed a task demanding self‑control, then a second similar task. The pooled results showed a very small self‑exhaustion effect; its 95 % confidence interval included 0 (d = 0.04, 95 % CI −0.07 to 0.15). Another replication, also preregistered, involved 36 labs and 3,531 participants and yielded d = 0.06 — again a negligible effect. These findings call into question the model that self‑control is a limited resource.
tips.sources: Hagger MS, Chatzisarantis NLD, Alberts H, et al. (2016). A Multilab Preregistered Replication of the Ego-Depletion Effect. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 11(4), 546–573. <https://doi.org/10.1177/1745691616652873>; Vohs et al. (2021). A Multisite Preregistered Paradigmatic Test of the Ego-Depletion Effect. Psychological Science. <https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797621989733>
tips.caveats: What’s being refuted is the notion that self‑control is a consumable resource, not that people can become fatigued. Lack of sleep or prolonged effort does reduce performance, but that falls under the guidelines on sleep and working hours in Section 3. The only evidence‑based actions are environmental tweaks and simple wording changes, as described in Section 4, items 10 (“move unwanted items out of reach”) and 1 (“write down exactly when, where and what you’ll do”). Fixing routine choices such as clothing and diet is still worthwhile because it costs almost nothing. It saves minutes and mental effort, not “willpower”; don’t expect it to improve your judgment later in the day. While other items in this section deal with monetary costs, this one concerns time and mental energy, which aren’t interchangeable.

tips.title: Don’t expect skipping breakfast or the 16:8 intermittent fasting method to help you control your weight; instead, pick a meal timing you can stick to long-term.
tips.cost: There’s no monetary cost. What you save is the mental energy you’d otherwise spend worrying about meal timing.
tips.inPlainWords: Popular belief holds that skipping breakfast leads to overeating at lunch and dinner, ultimately increasing total daily calorie intake. Research does not support this: people who skipped breakfast consumed over 200 fewer calories per day on average, and ended up slightly lighter. Compared to simply eating less overall, 16:8 intermittent fasting produces no meaningful difference in weight after a full year. That said, people who regularly skip breakfast do have a roughly 17% higher risk of cardiovascular disease; no significant difference in overall mortality has been observed, however.
tips.benefit: Let’s first address the claim that skipping breakfast causes people to eat more later in the day. One meta-analysis combined data from 13 randomized trials. Participants assigned to eat breakfast consumed 259.79 kcal more per day on average than those who skipped it (95% CI 78.87–440.71). Their body weight was also 0.44 kg higher (95% CI 0.07–0.82). However, people who skipped breakfast did not make up for those missing calories at subsequent meals. All these trials had very short follow-up periods: an average of 7 weeks for weight tracking, and just 2 weeks for measuring calorie intake. Next, we look at 16:8 intermittent fasting, which restricts eating to a specific window each day. One trial involved 116 overweight adults over 12 weeks. The group limited their eating to 12 p.m. to 8 p.m. showed no significant weight difference compared to those eating three regular meals daily: a difference of −0.26 kg (95% CI −1.30 to 0.78). Another trial conducted in Guangzhou followed 139 obese patients for 12 months. Those who combined time-restricted eating with calorie restriction lost 1.8 kg more on average than those only controlling calorie intake (95% CI −4.0 to 0.4), a difference that also failed to reach statistical significance. Finally, we examine whether long-term breakfast skipping is harmful. A pooled analysis of 2.38 million people found that skipping breakfast raised cardiovascular disease risk by 17% (OR 1.17, 95% CI 1.09–1.26), and cardiovascular-related mortality by 49% (OR 1.49, 95% CI 1.20–1.84). These findings come from observational studies that did not assign participants to breakfast or non-breakfast groups. One original study with 17–23 years of follow-up reported a 1.19-fold higher all-cause mortality risk for breakfast skippers (95% CI 0.99–1.42), a figure that crosses 1 but is not statistically significant.
tips.sources: Sievert K, Hussain SM, Page MJ, et al. (2019). Effect of breakfast on weight and energy intake: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. BMJ. <https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.l42>; Lowe DA, Wu N, Rohdin-Bibby L, et al. (2020). Effects of Time-Restricted Eating on Weight Loss and Other Metabolic Parameters in Women and Men With Overweight and Obesity. JAMA Internal Medicine. <https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2020.4153>; Liu D, Huang Y, Huang C, et al. (2022). Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss. New England Journal of Medicine. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2114833>; Zhang H, Zhang S, Liu Y, et al. (2025). The association between skipping breakfast and cardiovascular disease: a meta analysis. Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine. <https://doi.org/10.3389/fcvm.2025.1565806>; Rong S, Snetselaar LG, Xu G, et al. (2019). Association of Skipping Breakfast With Cardiovascular and All-Cause Mortality. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2019.01.065>; Fernandes-Alves D, Teixeira GP, Guimarães KC, Crispim CA (2026). Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials Comparing Time-Restricted Eating With and Without Caloric Restriction for Weight Loss. Nutrition Reviews. <https://doi.org/10.1093/nutrit/nuaf053>; Sun T, Zhang L, Lu Y, et al. (2024). Non-linear relationship between the first meal time of the day and gallstone incidence in American adults. Frontiers in Nutrition. <https://doi.org/10.3389/fnut.2024.1521707>; Liu T, Wang Y, Wang X, et al. (2023). Habitually Skipping Breakfast Is Associated with the Risk of Gastrointestinal Cancers: Evidence from the Kailuan Cohort Study. Journal of General Internal Medicine. <https://doi.org/10.1007/s11606-023-08094-7>
tips.caveats: This topic remains controversial. The 17% rise in cardiovascular disease risk stems from observational studies without controlled group assignments. Breakfast skippers also tend to smoke more, drink more alcohol, lead more sedentary lifestyles, and have lower incomes; these factors are not fully accounted for in the data, so it is unclear how much of this risk is directly attributable to skipping breakfast. The all-cause mortality finding also crosses 1 but lacks statistical significance. 16:8 intermittent fasting is similarly debated: a pooled analysis of 30 trials involving 1,341 participants showed that when both groups ate the same amount of food, the time-restricted eating group lost 1.46 kg more on average (95% CI −2.65 to −0.26), but at the cost of losing 0.41 kg more lean body mass. Most of these trials were very short in duration; the longest and most rigorous 12-month trial found no meaningful weight difference between the two groups. Prolonged fasting may also affect gallbladder health. One cross-sectional survey of 6,547 people found that for every hour later a person ate their first meal, their risk of gallstones rose by 5% (OR 1.05, 95% CI 1.02–1.08); those whose first meal was between 9 a.m. and 2 p.m. had a 49% higher risk compared to earlier eaters (OR 1.49, 95% CI 1.24–1.77). The underlying mechanism is that bile remains in the gallbladder longer, increasing the likelihood of stone formation. However, this is a cross-sectional study, so it is possible that existing gallbladder issues prompted people to change their eating habits. The very wide confidence interval for the latter figure indicates very few events occurred, so this should be viewed as a preliminary clue rather than conclusive evidence. Overall, when it comes to weight control, meal timing has minimal impact; there is no need to spend mental energy on this factor. As for whether long-term breakfast skipping is beneficial, all available evidence is correlational, not causal, but the trend leans toward negative outcomes. To be on the safe side, it is better to eat regular meals; don’t expect skipping breakfast to help you lose weight. The primary causes of gastritis and gastric ulcers are Helicobacter pylori infection and long-term use of painkillers; details are covered in Section 1, Item 23. For people who have gallstones detected via checkups but never experience pain, guidance is provided in Section 1, Item 20. To effectively control weight, proven strategies are eating enough fruits and vegetables (Section 2, Item 27), cutting back on ultra-processed foods (Section 2, Item 28), and keeping BMI within 20–25 (Section 2, Item 32). These recommendations do not apply to people with diabetes, those taking blood sugar-lowering medication, or pregnant individuals; skipping meals could lead to hypoglycemia in these groups, so they must follow their doctor’s instructions. Extreme fasting and induced vomiting are separate issues altogether; see Section 28, Item 1 for details.

tips.title: Don’t believe claims that masturbation harms health or that abstaining improves wellbeing; what really matters is whether it interferes with sleep, work, or relationships.
tips.cost: Zero. You save money you’d otherwise spend on dubious “kidney‑tonic” remedies, “abstinence” courses, and the chronic anxiety that comes from self‑blame.
tips.inPlainWords: No credible research shows masturbation harms health. One large U.S. study found men who ejaculated more often had roughly 20% fewer cases of prostate cancer. A British study, however, noted a higher risk among men who reported frequent ejaculation in their twenties and thirties, so neither figure should be taken as a health‑boosting prescription. Many people who feel “addicted” to pornography actually struggle because the behavior clashes with their personal moral beliefs.
tips.benefit: A U.S. study followed 31,925 men through 2010, asking each to report how often they ejaculated each month. Compared with men ejaculating 4–7 times monthly, those ejaculating more than 21 times had a hazard ratio of 0.81 (95% CI 0.72–0.92) for prostate cancer — a roughly 19% reduction — when the count was measured at ages 20–29. At ages 40–49 the ratio was 0.78 (0.69–0.89), a roughly 22% drop, mainly affecting low‑risk prostate cancers. A British case‑control study of 431 prostate‑cancer patients and 409 controls found a higher risk for men reporting frequent masturbation in their twenties and thirties, but a lower risk for those who reported it frequently after age 50. Regarding pornography, a meta‑analysis concluded that many people labeling themselves “addicted” are simply experiencing a conflict between their actions and personal values, rather than being driven solely by excessive exposure.
tips.sources: Rider JR, Wilson KM, Sinnott JA, et al. (2016). Ejaculation Frequency and Risk of Prostate Cancer: Updated Results with an Additional Decade of Follow-up. European Urology, 70(6), 974–982. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eururo.2016.03.027>; Dimitropoulou P, Lophatananon A, Easton D, et al. (2009). Sexual activity and prostate cancer risk in men diagnosed at a younger age. BJU International, 103(2), 178–185. <https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1464-410x.2008.08030.x>; Grubbs JB, Perry SL, Wilt JA, Reid RC. (2019). Pornography Problems Due to Moral Incongruence: An Integrative Model with a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Archives of Sexual Behavior, 48(2), 397–415. <https://doi.org/10.1007/s10508-018-1248-x>
tips.caveats: This topic remains controversial. Both prostate‑cancer studies merely observed correlations without controlled groups, and the frequency figures were self‑reported, so the evidence only supports the conclusion that there is no evidence of harm; it does not justify encouraging more frequent ejaculation. The British authors themselves note that the later‑age protective effect could reflect illness preceding reduced activity. The pornography meta‑analysis did not provide effect sizes, so only a directional trend is reported. The modest benefit rating reflects that the reduction applies mainly to low‑risk prostate cancers, not to mortality. Red flags that warrant a visit to a psychiatrist or psychologist include chronic sleep loss, missed work, damaged relationships, and an inability to cut back despite wanting to. For sleep issues, see Section 3, Item 9 (avoid staying up late for games, short videos, or porn). If you’re concerned about erectile problems linked to porn use, follow Section 1, Item 28: get a cardiovascular check‑up first. Legal consequences of sharing or selling pornographic material are outlined in Section 9, Item 4. Ultimately, the only person who benefits is you.

tips.title: Don’t spend money on “sexual orientation conversion” or “gay conversion therapy,” and don’t send your family members to such programs.
tips.cost: No cost at all. What you save is the money you would otherwise spend on conversion clinics, counseling centers, and the revenue generated by these “conversion” services. The real challenge is getting family members to accept that this isn’t necessary.
tips.inPlainWords: After reviewing relevant research, an expert panel from the American Psychological Association concluded that these conversion efforts cannot change a person’s sexual orientation and may actually cause harm. In one U.S. survey, nearly 90% of people who had undergone conversion therapy reported having suicidal thoughts.
tips.benefit: The 2009 APA task force report states that attempts to change sexual orientation “are unlikely to succeed and carry a certain risk of harm.” It also advises both parents and children to avoid any mandatory or inpatient conversion programs for minors. A nationwide U.S. survey of 1,518 LGBTQ+ adults found that about 7% had undergone conversion therapy; 80% of them were referred by religious figures. After adjusting for age and childhood trauma, people who had undergone conversion therapy had a 92% higher odds of having had suicidal thoughts at some point in their lives (OR 1.92, 95% CI 1.01–3.64). Their odds of having planned a suicide attempt were 75% higher (OR 1.75, 1.01–3.06), and their odds of attempting suicide without serious injury were 88% higher (OR 1.88, 1.01–3.50). Another study of 245 young adults aged 21–25 found that 22% of those who had never undergone conversion therapy attempted suicide; this figure rose to 48.1% among those whose parents tried to change their orientation, and to 62.8% among those whose parents sent them to therapists or religious figures for conversion. WHO’s ICD-10 classification explicitly states that “sexual orientation itself is not considered a disorder.”
tips.sources: American Psychological Association Task Force on Appropriate Therapeutic Responses to Sexual Orientation (2009). Report of the Task Force on Appropriate Therapeutic Responses to Sexual Orientation. <https://www.apa.org/pi/lgbt/resources/therapeutic-response.pdf>; Blosnich JR, Henderson ER, Coulter RWS, Goldbach JT, Meyer IH. (2020). Sexual Orientation Change Efforts, Adverse Childhood Experiences, and Suicide Ideation and Attempt Among Sexual Minority Adults, United States, 2016–2018. American Journal of Public Health, 110(7), 1024–1030. <https://doi.org/10.2105/AJPH.2020.305637>; Ryan C, Toomey RB, Diaz RM, Russell ST. (2020). Parent-Initiated Sexual Orientation Change Efforts With LGBT Adolescents: Implications for Young Adult Mental Health and Adjustment. Journal of Homosexuality, 67(2), 159–173. <https://doi.org/10.1080/00918369.2018.1538407>; World Health Organization. Sexual Orientation Change Efforts Do Not Increase Suicide: Correcting a False Research Narrative. Archives of Sexual Behavior, 51, 3377–3393. <https://doi.org/10.1007/s10508-022-02408-2>; Blosnich JR, Coulter RWS, Henderson ER, et al. (2023). tips.caveats: This topic remains controversial. In 2022, Sullins reanalyzed the same dataset while excluding participants who already reported suicidal thoughts prior to conversion therapy; this analysis showed no significant link between conversion therapy and suicidal thoughts (OR 0.44, 0.20–0.94). Sullins’ organization opposes LGBTQ+ rights, and the original study authors have responded to these findings. While the extent of harm caused by conversion therapy is still debated, there is no credible evidence contradicting the fact that such therapy cannot change sexual orientation. This study was assigned a Grade B rating because all data on potential harm were collected via retrospective self-report surveys. Legally, the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 sets the only route for admitting an adult to a psychiatric facility against their wishes, and it is narrower than “seems to be a risk”. Admission as a supported patient under section 89, for up to thirty days, requires two independent examinations — one by a psychiatrist, the other by a psychiatrist, a mental health professional or a medical practitioner — each concluding that the person has a mental illness of such severity that they have recently threatened, attempted or are threatening to cause bodily harm to themselves, or have recently behaved violently towards another person or caused another person to fear bodily harm, or are unable to care for themselves to a degree that places them at risk of harm. It also requires that admission is the least restrictive option available, that the person is unable to make mental healthcare decisions independently and needs very high support, and that a nominated representative is appointed. Anyone admitted without that paperwork can challenge the admission before the Mental Health Review Board. No Indian statute bans conversion therapy outright; the Indian Psychiatric Society's position and the National Medical Commission's professional-conduct regulations treat it as improper practice rather than a criminal offence, so the protection here is professional discipline and civil liability, not prosecution. Individuals struggling emotionally due to this issue may seek help from psychiatrists or clinical psychologists to alleviate their distress. Guidance on how families should respond after a child comes out is provided in Section 30, Item 15 (“When a child says they’re attracted to the same sex”). The primary beneficiaries of avoiding conversion therapy are both you and your family members.

tips.title: Do not expect "proper lifting technique" or manual handling training to prevent back pain; real prevention comes from reducing lifted load and frequency, combined with regular exercise
tips.cost: Zero financial cost. You stop stressing over whether your back is bent while lifting and avoid wasting money on back belts or ergonomic posture seminars. What is required is breaking heavy loads into smaller portions, using dollies/trolleys, asking for assistance, and sustaining regular weekly exercise.
tips.inPlainWords: Workers who undergo training in "correct lifting posture" experience just as much back pain as those who receive no training. People who flex their spine while lifting are no more likely to develop back pain than those who keep it straight. What genuinely correlates with back pain is the sheer weight and frequency of lifting: every extra 10 kg lifted or extra 10 lifts per day raises risk by about 10%. Maintaining regular exercise cuts back pain recurrences by 35% to 45%.
tips.benefit: A Cochrane systematic review pooling 9 randomized trials with 20,101 employees evaluated manual handling advice and assistive devices: workers who received training had virtually identical back pain rates compared to control groups receiving no intervention (OR 1.17, 95% CI 0.68–2.02, moderate certainty). Compared with simple video education, training showed no advantage (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.69–1.25). The authors concluded that manual handling training alone does not prevent back pain or related disability. Regarding spinal flexion, a 2020 systematic review in JOSPT found no evidence linking greater lumbar spine flexion during lifting to low back pain; in prospective cohorts, the maximum lumbar flexion angle between workers who developed back pain and those who remained pain-free differed by only 1.5 degrees (not significant). In 7 studies measuring flexion differently, people with back pain actually flexed their spine 6.0 degrees less than pain-free individuals. Conversely, an occupational meta-analysis of 8 prospective studies found that heavier and more frequent lifting is significantly associated with back pain: every additional 10 kg lifted increased risk by 11% (OR 1.11, 95% CI 1.05–1.18), and every 10 additional lifts per day increased risk by 9% (OR 1.09, 95% CI 1.03–1.15). A JAMA Internal Medicine meta-analysis of 21 randomized trials (30,850 participants) showed that exercise combined with education reduced the risk of back pain episodes by 45% (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.41–0.74, moderate certainty), while exercise alone reduced episodes by 35% (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.50–0.86). Education alone had no effect (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.83–1.27), and back support belts showed zero benefit (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.71–1.44). The UK Health and Safety Executive (HSE) explicitly states that training alone cannot overcome hazardous manual handling operations or replace mechanical lifting equipment.

tips.title: Do not expect megadosing calcium or drinking bone broth after a bone fracture to accelerate bone healing
tips.cost: Zero financial cost, while saving money spent on high-dose supplements, special tonics, and tedious bone broth preparation. All that is required is supplementing only if clinical deficiency is diagnosed.
tips.inPlainWords: Randomized clinical trials testing vitamin D supplementation after bone fractures show zero improvement in bone healing rates or functional recovery. The amount of calcium extracted into a large bowl of animal bone broth represents less than 5% of daily recommended calcium intake. Unless a doctor diagnoses pre-existing deficiency or osteoporosis, megadosing supplements provides no advantage and raises kidney stone risks.
tips.benefit: A 2023 systematic review examining 14 studies (2,734 fracture patients) concluded that vitamin D supplementation had negligible effects on radiological union, non-union rates, and post-recovery functional outcomes. Across randomized double-blind trials specifically, none demonstrated clinical benefit. In a trial of 100 long-bone fracture patients with low vitamin D receiving a single mega-dose (100,000 IU) versus placebo within two weeks of injury, non-union rates were identical (2 patients in each arm, 4% total). In another trial of 102 femur or tibia fracture patients randomized across four dosage tiers or placebo, healing scores showed zero difference at 3 and 12 months. In a high-resolution imaging trial of 32 postmenopausal distal radius fracture patients, high-dose daily vitamin D (1,800 IU) actually resulted in lower compressive bone stiffness at the fracture site compared to control. Regarding bone broth, chemical analysis of commercial and home-prepared bone broths found that a standard 450–550 g bowl contains only 14 to 39 mg of calcium—a mere 1.4% to 3.9% of the 1,000 mg recommended daily intake. National dietary guidelines warn that excessive calcium intake increases nephrolithiasis (kidney stone) risk. In the Women's Health Initiative trial of 36,282 postmenopausal women followed for 7 years, taking 1,000 mg calcium plus 400 IU vitamin D daily elevated kidney stone risk by 17% (HR 1.17, 95% CI 1.02–1.34), without significantly reducing hip fractures (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.72–1.08).

tips.title: Do not rely on AI chatbots to independently diagnose medical conditions or resolve legal disputes; verify primary citations before seeking care, litigating, or spending money
tips.cost: Zero financial cost. Verification requires a few minutes to half an hour to request the specific statutory section, clinical guideline, or academic citation from the model, and then consult the primary text directly. The habit to break is unquestioning obedience to fluent, confident model outputs.
tips.inPlainWords: When provided with a complete, structured medical record, large language models identify the underlying illness over 90% of the time. However, when everyday users consult AI chatbots regarding their own symptoms, they diagnose conditions less accurately than people searching standard medical websites, and are no better at deciding whether to visit the emergency department. On legal questions, general-purpose LLMs hallucinate inaccurate citations in 58% to 88% of queries and readily adopt erroneous premises introduced by the user.
tips.benefit: In a 2026 preregistered randomized study published in Nature Medicine involving 1,298 UK laypeople, participants evaluated clinical scenarios requiring diagnostic and triage decisions. Participants assisted by leading AI models (GPT-4o, Llama 3, Command R+) were compared against a control group using standard web searches (primarily NHS.uk). When the complete medical case was fed directly to AI, the models correctly identified the condition in 94.9% of cases and selected the proper triage level in 56.3%. However, when everyday participants interacted with those same models, diagnostic accuracy plunged below 34.5% and triage accuracy fell below 44.2%. Control participants searching standard resources were 1.76 times more likely to identify the correct condition (95% CI 1.45–2.13) and 1.57 times more likely to identify red-flag conditions (95% CI 1.28–1.92). Chat logs revealed failure points at both ends: lay users frequently omitted critical clinical nuances, and users often dismissed the model when it did propose the correct diagnosis. In the legal domain, a Stanford empirical study (2024) evaluated general-purpose LLMs against federal court case law: ChatGPT-4 exhibited hallucinations in 58% of legal queries, while Llama 2 hallucinated in 88% of cases. When queries incorporated flawed legal assumptions, models sycophantically confirmed the user's premise. A follow-up 2025 study evaluating specialized commercial legal AI tools found hallucinations occurred in 17% to 33% of complex research queries.

However, that study evaluated response tone and composition rather than patient comprehension or diagnostic outcomes. Benchmarks on static exam questions do not predict lay user performance. Model hallucinations stem from next-token training dynamics where guessing produces partial reward, while acknowledging uncertainty receives no reward. To audit AI outputs, ask the model to provide the exact title and article number of the statutory code, guideline, or peer-reviewed DOI, then verify the exact sentence in official databases. Prompt objectively ("What does statutory law specify in this situation?") rather than seeking affirmation ("Am I guaranteed to win this case?"). Critical red flags like sudden facial droop, unilateral arm weakness, or crushing chest pain require immediate emergency services, not chatbot triage (see Chapter 13, Item 3 and 7). Legal aid options are outlined in Chapter 7, Item 3. Benefit magnitude is categorized as Low due to surrogate accuracy endpoints. Primary beneficiaries are yourself and your family.

tips.title: Do not stop saving money on the premise that "anyone could die at any moment so spend it all now"; in India about 84% of thirty-year-olds survive to age sixty
tips.cost: Zero financial cost. What is required is pausing when the thought arises ("who knows if I'll even be here tomorrow?") and considering the objective probability of surviving to sixty. The difficulty is that peer culture frequently normalizes nihilistic spending, while desired consumer items are right in front of you.
tips.inPlainWords: Younger individuals systematically overestimate their probability of premature death; living according to this distorted subjective risk leads young adults to save roughly 26% less than rational lifecycle models dictate. Most people will live to old age and need accumulated savings to support those decades.
tips.benefit: The relevant life tables are India's own. In the World Health Organization's 2023 life tables for India, 84.4% of thirty-year-olds reach age 60 (81.4% of males, 87.6% of females), 73.4% of all Indians reach age 65 (69.6% of males, 77.4% of females), and 40.6% reach age 80 (34.7% of males, 47.0% of females). Those who reach 65 live 15.3 more years on average. Indian life expectancy at birth is about 70 years — 69.9 in the Sample Registration System's tables for 2018-22 — lower than in high-income countries, which is why roughly a quarter of Indians die before 65. Regarding subjective perception, a 2019 study published in The Journal of Finance surveyed subjective survival beliefs: younger adults dramatically underestimate their probability of survival, whereas older adults overestimate theirs. For instance, a 28-year-old male with an actuarial 99.4% probability of surviving the next five years subjectively estimated his survival probability at only 92.8%. When researchers integrated these distorted subjective survival expectations into standard life-cycle consumption and savings models, younger adults saved 26% less than optimal, while retirees decumulated wealth 27% too slowly. The more distorted an individual's mortality beliefs, the more skewed their savings behavior remained, even after controlling for risk aversion, cognitive ability, and household income. The authors identified availability bias—overweighting sensationalized, highly salient causes of premature death—as a key psychological driver.

tips.title: Do not undergo arthroscopic debridement or partial meniscectomy for gradual knee pain in older adults (osteoarthritis or degenerative meniscal tears); prioritize weight loss and quadriceps strengthening first
tips.cost: Zero cost for surgery, avoiding 2 to 6 weeks of postoperative rehabilitation downtime. Requires dedicating time several days a week for long-term lower limb muscle strengthening, ideally taught by a physical therapist. Overweight individuals also need caloric restriction. The difficulty is that exercise and weight loss require sustained discipline, while surgery promises an enticing "one-time fix."
tips.inPlainWords: For middle-aged and older adults suffering from gradual degenerative knee pain, undergoing arthroscopic joint "cleanup" or partial meniscus resection performs no better than sham (placebo) surgery. In sham surgery, doctors merely made superficial skin incisions without inserting arthroscopic instruments, yet patients experienced identical pain relief and functional recovery. Any perceived surgical benefits fade within months, while the procedure carries risks of deep vein thrombosis. Strengthening leg muscles and shedding excess weight reliably reduce knee pain.
tips.benefit: Regarding osteoarthritis, a landmark 2002 NEJM trial randomized 180 knee osteoarthritis patients across three arms: arthroscopic debridement, arthroscopic lavage, or sham surgery (skin incisions only, without intra-articular scope insertion). Patients and evaluators were completely blinded. Across two years of scheduled follow-ups, neither genuine surgical procedure provided superior pain relief or functional recovery over sham surgery (1-year knee pain score [0–100 scale]: sham 48.9, lavage 54.8, debridement 51.7). A 2008 NEJM trial of 178 moderate-to-severe knee osteoarthritis patients randomized participants to arthroscopic debridement plus physical therapy/medication versus physical therapy/medication alone: after two years, total symptom scores (0–2,400 scale) were 874 vs 897 (difference 23 points, 95% CI -208 to 161, non-significant). Regarding meniscal tears, a 2013 NEJM Finnish trial evaluated 146 patients aged 35–65 with degenerative medial meniscus tears without osteoarthritis: arthroscopic partial meniscectomy showed zero statistically significant difference over sham surgery at 12 months across knee pain during exercise (-3.1 vs -3.3 points) and functional indices. A 2015 BMJ meta-analysis pooling 9 trials found arthroscopy provided a small 3 to 5 point pain reduction (0–100 scale) at 3 to 6 months that vanished by 1 to 2 years, with zero long-term functional improvement. Harms included deep vein thrombosis (4.13 events per 1,000 procedures, 95% CI 1.78–9.60), pulmonary embolism, infection, and death. In 2017, a BMJ international expert panel issued a strong recommendation against arthroscopy for almost all patients with degenerative knee disease. Regarding alternatives, a 2016 Norwegian trial of 140 middle-aged patients with degenerative meniscal tears randomized to 12 weeks of supervised exercise versus arthroscopic surgery found identical 2-year knee outcomes (difference 0.9 points), with the exercise cohort demonstrating superior muscle strength at 3 months. A Cochrane systematic review of 44 trials (3,537 patients) confirmed exercise reduced knee pain by 12 points (0–100 scale, high-quality evidence), maintaining 6-point reductions months after cessation. In the IDEA trial of 454 overweight/obese knee osteoarthritis patients aged >=55, combined intensive diet and exercise resulted in average 10.6 kg weight loss (11.4% body weight) and significantly lower pain scores at 18 months (3.6 vs 4.7 on 0–20 scale) compared to exercise alone.

tips.title: Do not expect melatonin to cure chronic insomnia; it advances sleep onset by an average of only 7 minutes—prioritize cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia instead
tips.cost: Zero financial cost; saves money spent on ongoing commercial melatonin purchases. The difficulty is convenience: swallowing an over-the-counter gummy or pill is far easier than committing to weeks of clinical behavioral restructuring.
tips.inPlainWords: For individuals struggling with insomnia, taking melatonin advances sleep onset by an average of roughly 7 minutes and extends total sleep duration by only about 8 minutes compared to placebo. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine advises against using melatonin to treat chronic insomnia.
tips.benefit: A 2013 meta-analysis pooled 19 randomized, placebo-controlled trials involving 1,683 participants with primary sleep disorders (including 14 trials specifically on insomnia): melatonin reduced sleep onset latency by an average of 7.06 minutes (95% CI 4.37–9.75), increased total sleep time by 8.25 minutes (95% CI 1.74–14.75), and produced a negligible improvement in sleep quality (SMD 0.22, 95% CI 0.12–0.32), lagging substantially behind prescription sleep aids. In clinical practice guidelines for chronic insomnia issued by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM, 2017), the panel issued a "weak" recommendation against clinicians using melatonin for sleep onset or sleep maintenance insomnia, evaluating trials in adults aged >=55 and judging the overall evidence quality as "very low" with pooled sleep quality improvements failing to meet clinical significance thresholds (SMD 0.21, 95% CI -0.36 to 0.77). In contrast, for acute circadian shifts, a Cochrane systematic review of 10 randomized trials demonstrated that taking 0.5 to 5 mg of melatonin near local bedtime after flying across five or more time zones significantly reduces jet lag symptoms compared to placebo. Melatonin appears deceptively appealing because it is an endogenous pineal hormone perceived as harmless and available without prescription.

Authors of the 2013 meta-analysis noted that melatonin exhibits minimal tolerance and low adverse events, suggesting a modest adjunctive role. However, trial data in older adults demonstrate that the absolute benefit is simply too small to resolve clinical insomnia disorder. First-line therapy for chronic insomnia is CBT-I, detailed in Chapter 3, Item 26. Snoring and daytime drowsiness warrant screening for obstructive sleep apnea (Chapter 3, Item 27). tips.title: Do not demand intravenous (IV) drips for common colds or uncomplicated fevers, and never receive seasonal IV infusions to "flush" or "clear" blood vessels
tips.cost: Zero financial cost; saves money spent on clinic drip fees and hours spent sitting in infusion clinics. The challenge is overcoming the cultural misconception that "an IV drip cures illnesses faster," and breaking habits among seniors who request seasonal preventive infusions.
tips.inPlainWords: A drip is a medical procedure with real risks, not a tonic. No infusion of saline, vitamins or “antioxidants” flushes away or dissolves the plaques in your arteries; the artery wall is protected over years by blood pressure and lipid control. Extra intravenous fluid strains the heart and kidneys, and can precipitate heart failure in someone with heart disease. Indian guidance on rational use of medicines and antibiotic stewardship points the same way - a common cold or an uncomplicated viral throat infection does not need an outpatient infusion - but clinics and “wellness” centres sell them anyway, which is why you have to ask what the drip is for.
tips.benefit: The principle is simple and the World Health Organization states it plainly: never inject when oral medication is possible; never infuse intravenously when intramuscular injection is possible. An intravenous infusion is clinically justified in three situations: an inability to swallow; severe gastrointestinal malabsorption, with persistent vomiting or severe diarrhoea; or a critical, rapidly progressing illness that needs a high drug concentration in the blood at once. A common cold, an uncomplicated sore throat or a seasonal “flush” is none of those. Infusions cannot dislodge or clear atherosclerotic plaques; unindicated fluid loading risks circulatory volume overload, cardiac strain and acute heart failure. India has no nationwide directive that designates outpatient drip clinics off limits. The standard comes instead from professional regulation: the National Medical Commission's professional-conduct regulations require the rational use of medicines, hospital antimicrobial-stewardship committees review what is prescribed, and the Pharmacovigilance Programme of India collects reports of adverse drug reactions — in which injections feature far more heavily than oral medicines.

tips.caveats: Rated Grade C because findings derive from regulatory directives and expert consensus rather than randomized non-infusion clinical trials. Genuine medical emergencies (such as severe hypovolemic dehydration, septic shock, or inability to retain fluids) require indicated IV therapy under physician supervision. Demanding unneeded antibiotics for viral colds is also ineffective, detailed in Chapter 34, Item 7. For dehydration from diarrhea, oral rehydration salts are the first-line standard (Chapter 34, Item 8). Genuine stroke prevention relies on blood pressure and lipid control through consistent oral maintenance therapy, as detailed in Chapter 1, Item 7, and Chapter 2, Item 12. Benefit magnitude is categorized as Low based on financial savings and avoiding infusion site infections or allergic reactions. Primary beneficiaries are yourself and elderly family members.
